title: Ezekiel 14:1–11
context: Ezekiel reports that some elders of Israel came and sat before him. The LORD tells him that these men have taken idols into their hearts and asks whether he should be inquired of by them at all. Anyone who cherishes idols and comes to a prophet will be answered by the LORD himself. The LORD calls the house of Israel to return and turn from their idols. If a prophet is deceived and speaks, the LORD says he has deceived that prophet, and both prophet and inquirer will bear their iniquity, so that Israel may no longer go astray but be his people. Both traditions read the call to repentance as sincere, and both hold the false prophet and the inquirer responsible.

verses.text: Then some of the elders of Israel came to me and sat before me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel reports that some elders of Israel came and sat before him. They come to inquire.

Arminian readers see leaders who seek the prophet while their hearts remain divided, as the following verses reveal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elders also sit before Ezekiel in 8:1 (there called “the elders of Judah”) and in 20:1.

Reformed readers see outward inquiry without inward devotion. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the gap that can open between religious form and the heart.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. God responds before the elders speak.

Arminian readers see God addressing the inquirers’ real condition rather than their stated request, which the text does not record.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text gives no record of what the elders asked.

Reformed readers see God knowing hearts before words are spoken. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s knowledge of those who come to him and his concern with the heart behind the inquiry.

verses.text: “Son of man, these men have taken their idols into their heart, and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face. Should I be inquired of at all by them?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says these men have taken idols into their hearts and set a stumbling block before their faces, and asks, “Should I be inquired of at all by them?” Inner idolatry is exposed.

Arminian readers see divided loyalty that undermines inquiry.
verses.reformedNotes:
The idols may be inward attachments rather than physical images; readers differ.

Reformed readers see the heart as the seat of idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Therefore speak to them and tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Every man of the house of Israel who takes his idols into his heart and puts the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face then comes to the prophet, I the LORD will answer him there according to the multitude of his idols,
verses.arminianNotes:
Anyone in Israel who takes idols into his heart and comes to the prophet will be answered by the LORD according to his idols. God responds directly.

Arminian readers see consequences matching the heart’s choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The answer is not a normal oracle but God’s own response to their idolatry.

Reformed readers see God judging the heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God refusing to be used by those who cherish idols.

verses.text: that I may take the house of Israel in their own heart, because they are all estranged from me through their idols.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
God will do this to take hold of Israel in their own heart, because they are estranged from him through their idols. The aim is the heart.

Arminian readers see God seeking to win back his estranged people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse suggests that the judgment is meant to recover the people, not only punish them.

Reformed readers see God laying hold of the heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s desire for wholehearted devotion rather than divided loyalty.

verses.text: “Therefore tell the house of Israel, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Return, and turn yourselves from your idols! Turn away your faces from all your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD calls Israel: “Return, and turn yourselves from your idols!” A call to repentance stands at the center.

Arminian readers see a sincere call that people are enabled to answer.
verses.reformedNotes:
The call to turn is repeated in 18:32 and 33:11.

Reformed readers see the command to repent as real, with turning made effective by God’s grace. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the sincerity of God’s call to repent.

verses.text: “ ‘ “For everyone of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live in Israel, who separates himself from me and takes his idols into his heart, and puts the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire for himself of me, I the LORD will answer him by myself.
verses.arminianNotes:
Anyone in Israel, or any stranger living there, who separates himself from God, takes idols into his heart, and inquires of the prophet will be answered by the LORD himself. The warning includes resident foreigners.

Arminian readers see personal accountability for all.
verses.reformedNotes:
The inclusion of strangers shows the covenant standard applies to all who live among Israel.

Reformed readers see God answering idolatry directly. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will set my face against that man and will make him an astonishment, for a sign and a proverb, and I will cut him off from among my people. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will set his face against such a man, make him a sign and a proverb, and cut him off from his people. The consequence is severe.

Arminian readers see judgment meant to warn others away from idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes:
Being made a sign suggests that the judgment serves as public warning.

Reformed readers see God’s holiness judging idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of idolatry and its consequences within the covenant community.

verses.text: “ ‘ “If the prophet is deceived and speaks a word, I, the LORD, have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand on him, and will destroy him from among my people Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
If a prophet is deceived and speaks, “I, the LORD, have deceived that prophet,” and God will destroy him. The verse attributes the deception to God.

Arminian readers see judicial hardening of one who already chose falsehood.
verses.reformedNotes:
Compare 1 Kings 22:22–23. On how God relates to deception and evil agents, see the box at Judges 9:23.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign judgment through deception without God being its author. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: They will bear their iniquity. The iniquity of the prophet will be even as the iniquity of him who seeks him,
verses.arminianNotes:
They will bear their iniquity; the prophet’s guilt will be as that of the one who sought him. Both are responsible.

Arminian readers see shared accountability between the false prophet and the inquirer who wanted a convenient answer.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse makes clear that the deceived prophet is not excused.

Reformed readers see God holding both parties responsible. Both traditions read this as shared ground about human responsibility, even where God’s judgment is at work in the deception.

verses.text: that the house of Israel may no more go astray from me, neither defile themselves any more with all their transgressions; but that they may be my people, and I may be their God,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The purpose is that Israel may no longer go astray or defile themselves, but be God’s people, and he their God. Judgment serves restoration.

Arminian readers see God’s goal of a faithful people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The covenant formula appears again, as in 11:20.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose to restore his people through judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s aim of a purified people who belong to him and he to them.
